extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, advocacy organizations, and other stakeholders who want to submit public comments on federal proposed regulations
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for drafting effective public comments during federal notice-and-comment rulemaking, including what to include, how to support arguments, and procedural requirements (e.g., citations, deadlines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who can comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Any member of the public (private individuals, organizations and associations on behalf of their members, etc.) can submit a public comment. Comments can be submitted anonymously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes individuals and organizations; anonymous submissions are allowed. Use this to understand eligibility and participation rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: What a comment is (purpose/role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments do not function as votes for or against a rule. Rather, they provide the government with relevant, detailed, and reliable opinions informed by the professional and personal experiences of the commentators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective comments build a record of opinion, inform the agency about unforeseen impacts, and refute or affirm assumptions relied upon by the agency. Comments that address methodology, assumptions, or reasoning can require agencies to provide a reasoned response and may support judicial challenges if ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadline awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies specify a deadline for comments—typically there is a 30 to 60 day window for comments when a proposed rule is posted online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the docket or Regulations.gov posting and submit within the specified comment period; late comments are usually not considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: No required structure or word limit
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no required structure or word limit when writing a comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although there's no formal format, following suggested components (introduction, background, analysis, recommendations, conclusion) makes comments more useful to agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested component — Introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Explains why you are interested in the regulation and highlights the personal or professional experience(s) that inform your opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the introduction to frame your perspective and establish why your input is relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested component — Background
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifies the part(s) of the regulation you are commenting on, and clearly states your opposition or support for each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference specific sections/subparts so agencies can link your feedback to particular provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested component — Recommendation(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offers suggestions on specific changes you would make to the proposed rule; recommendations could be to not proceed with the entire rule or to change specific sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete, actionable recommendations are more helpful than general complaints; explain the precise text or approach you want changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested component — Arguments and Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Explains how the proposed rule might impact you personally and/or professionally, whether the agency relied on incorrect information, unintended consequences of the proposed rule that were not considered, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed reasoning and evidence tying the rule to real-world effects; explain assumptions the agency made that you dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested component — Conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarizes your main argument and re-lists your recommendations. Remind the agency whether you support or oppose their proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the conclusion to reiterate the action you want the agency to take and the key reasons it should do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the regulation before commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the regulation before commenting: read the introduction/background where the agency lays out purpose and applicable laws, the agency's justifications, and the proposed rule text (often at the end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search and read proposed regulations on Regulations.gov; use agency, RIN, or keywords to find the correct docket. Understanding the document helps you reference specific reasoning or text to critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take a clear stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly state whether you agree with or disagree with the proposed rule (or an aspect of it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You do not have to comment on every issue raised by a rule; focus on the issues you understand best and that concern you most.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get specific — explain rationale and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: After you state support or opposition, specifically explain the rationale behind your opinion and emphasize how the rule would have a positive or negative impact on your specific situation or overall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific and substantive comments are more likely to require responses from an agency; tie claims to concrete harms, benefits, or factual errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name your experience or expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the credentials and experiences that distinguish you from other commenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You do not have to be a legal or scientific expert—clearly stating relevant experience (professional, occupational, or lived experience) increases credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Back up your opinions with sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, refer to multiple sources (personal insights and/or quantitative data-driven facts) to support your comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite studies, data, reports, or other evidence that substantiate your claims; combine with anecdotal experience when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak from your perspective (relevant industry or role)
rubrics_metrics.description: State if you are part of a relevant industry or group affected by the rule (science, agriculture, business, etc.) and draw from that experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear how your role or industry connection informs the likely impacts of the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on 'on the ground' experience when applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have direct operational or lived experience with the subject matter or impact of the rule, draw from that experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Firsthand operational insights can reveal practical consequences the agency may have overlooked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite the proposed rule precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: All comments must include the agency name and docket or RIN. If commenting on a particular subpart or section, reference the heading and page number of that subpart or section from the Federal Register document; for words/phrases, provide page and paragraph citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precise citations let agencies locate the provision you address and make it easier for them to respond to specific points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer alternative options
rubrics_metrics.description: If you disagree with the rule (or a section of it), suggest an alternative and explain how the alternative is more effective or better meets the same policy objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives can range from text edits to recommending that the agency not proceed with the rule; explain why your alternative better achieves the statute's goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address opposing views and trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: If able, address trade-offs or counter opposing views in your comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipating and rebutting counterarguments strengthens your submission and helps the agency weigh competing interests.
